67.title: Kosovo's Neighbours: The Border Crossing
67.summary: Explains that Kosovo borders Albania, North Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro, and that a border crossing is where police check people, vehicles and goods and ask for passports and documents. The opening photo shows a driver handing his documents to a border police officer; pupils are asked what the officer is doing. Named crossings include Qafë-Morina, Qafë-Prushi and Morina (to Albania) and Kulla (to Montenegro), each flying both countries' flags.

68.title: Activity: We Celebrate Kosovo's Independence
68.summary: Recounts how Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008 after years of peaceful resistance led by president Ibrahim Rugova and armed resistance by the Kosovo Liberation Army, honouring fallen fighters such as Adem Jashari. Pupils then celebrate in class: decorate with the Kosovo flag, dress in blue, white and yellow, stand for the anthem, and set up corners — a photo exhibition of those who fought, a sweets corner, a gallery of drawings, a quiz corner and a music-and-dance corner.

69.title: The Family Then and Now
69.summary: A father sitting by the fireplace remembers his childhood village house where 27 relatives lived under one roof, the grandfather made all decisions, women cooked and ate last, and there was no running water or electricity (candles and oil lamps). Today he lives in the city of Peja and is cooking dinner for his wife, a doctor, and his student daughter who is driving from Prishtina after picking up her brother at the airport. The lesson contrasts the traditional extended, patriarchal family with the modern two-generation family where parents share decisions and chores.

70.title: The Village Then and Now
70.summary: Pupils compare photographs of a village in the past and today and fill in a then / in common / now chart. In the past villages had small houses, big families, land worked with a plough, no electricity, running water or nearby schools; today they have large modern houses, modern farm machinery, well-equipped animal farms, electricity, water supply and asphalt roads. Pictures should contrast old and modern village life, farming and livestock.

71.title: The City Then and Now
71.summary: Klea, who lives in Prishtina, sits with her grandfather in the neighbourhood park while he describes the city of the past: smaller, few vehicles, low buildings far apart, craftsmen such as blacksmiths, carpenters, shoemakers, tailors and plis (felt cap) makers, small shops and green parks. Today the city has dense tall buildings, shopping centres, heavy traffic, wide roads and little greenery, plus many public and private schools, kindergartens and hospitals. Pictures illustrate the old versus modern city.

72.title: Branches of the Economy
72.summary: A teacher asks pupils to write what comes to mind when they hear the word 'economy' and then writes their ideas on the board. The full-page illustration shows a blonde teacher writing on a blackboard: economy means production, countries with developed economies are rich, many people are employed, and the branches are industry, agriculture, livestock farming, viticulture, trade and tourism.

73.title: Branches of the Economy (continued)
73.summary: Pupils fill in a table with family members' names, their professions and the branch of the economy each belongs to, then compare with a classmate. The text defines the economy and its branches: agriculture, livestock and fishing (food products); industry (factories, workshops, mines); and trade, hospitality and tourism. It notes that work once done by many workers with primitive tools is now done by fewer workers with specialised machines.

74.title: My Country and the Economy
74.summary: Two children, Mira and Nili, play a knowledge game called 'The economy of my country': Mira writes about village work and Nili about city work. In villages people farm grain, fruit and vegetables (once with a wooden plough, now with modern machinery) and raise animals and poultry on modern farms; in cities people work in factories, workshops and mines, in shops and shopping centres stocked with local and imported goods, and in crafts. Pictures illustrate rural farming versus urban industry and trade.

75.title: My Country and the Economy (continued)
75.summary: Discussion questions about why people work and which branches are developed in villages, cities and Kosovo. The text describes Kosovo's economy: farming (fruit, vegetables, grain), livestock (sheep and cows for meat and dairy), electricity produced from coal, small private industry, trade, winter tourism in the Sharr mountains (Brezovica, Prevalla) and the Accursed Mountains (Boga), and banks.

76.title: People Who Are Not Forgotten
76.summary: Introduces people who helped open Albanian-language schools in Kosovo: Ernest Koliqi, who brought teachers from Albania; teachers such as Mehmet Gjevori, Tajar Hatipi, Vezire Xherina and Beqir Kastrati; Mati Logoreci, first teacher at the Albanian Boys' School in Prizren; and Sevasti Qiriazi, pioneer of education for women. Pictures are portraits of these educators; pupils name schools and educators from their own town.

77.title: People Who Are Not Forgotten: Doctors
77.summary: A boy named Mali, who likes visiting his gentle dentist, asks his grandfather what medicine was like in his day. Grandfather explains there were few doctors, they had to study abroad, and names early Kosovo doctors (Dr Tefik Rashiti, Dr Xheladin Deda, Dr Ali Sokoli, first gynaecologist Dr Sehadete Mekuli). The text then credits teachers, doctors and economists for the country's progress and mentions the ministries of education and health and the University of Prishtina.

78.title: Culture — A National Treasure
78.summary: Klea's class researches people who contributed to sport and the arts and presents in groups. Group one covers team sports, focusing on football with a photo of footballer Fadil Vokrri; group two covers individual sports with a photo of judoka Majlinda Kelmendi, who won Kosovo's first world judo title and many gold medals.

79.title: Culture — A National Treasure: Music, Film, Painting
79.summary: Group three presents music in Kosovo: folk singer Ymer Riza with sharki and çifteli (traditional string instruments), singer and actress Nexhmije Pagarusha ('the Nightingale of Kosovo'), and world-famous pop singers Rita Ora and Dua Lipa. Group four presents theatre and film (the National Theatre of Kosovo founded 1946, actor Bekim Fehmiu who played in over 40 films) and painting. Pictures are portraits of these artists.

80.title: Culture — A National Treasure (conclusion)
80.summary: Shows the painting 'The Rooster' (Gjeli) by Engjëll Berisha, 1996, as an example of Kosovo art. Pupils discuss whether Kosovo has a developed culture and research other sports, music genres and well-known local names. The text says sport, music, theatre, film and painting show Kosovo's rich culture, handed down through generations.

81.title: Meeting: Learning from Our Notable People
81.summary: A class activity: invite a well-known local person (doctor, economist, businessperson, athlete, musician, veteran teacher) and write six interview questions to learn about their life and work, asking for a message to the young. Alternatively, make a photo exhibition of notable people, and sort name labels into categories: athlete, doctor, singer, actor, teacher, businessperson, fighter.

82.title: We Preserve Our Traditions
82.summary: Mali and his parents visit old family friends in the city of Shkodra, Albania, where he tastes a traditional dish he has never eaten and is struck by the hosts' warm hospitality and humour; they are served tea and sweets. He befriends the family's son Tomor, who shares all his toys, and on the drive home his father explains that Albanians inherited this tradition of hospitality from their ancestors. Pictures illustrate a welcoming home visit and traditional food.

83.title: We Preserve Our Traditions (continued)
83.summary: Pupils discuss photographs in groups and name three traditional foods, three elements of national tradition and the meaning of 'hospitality'. The text defines culture and tradition (language, music, customs, architecture, house arrangement, festivities, cooking) and notes that Albanians are known for their traditional weddings. Pictures show traditional foods and customs.

84.title: Cultures Are Diverse
84.summary: At Andrra's birthday party, a boy named Joni admires the paintings on the walls showing men in white plis caps and women in colourful traditional dress, shelves of books by great Albanian authors (the Frashëri brothers, Gjergj Fishta, Asdreni, Ismail Kadare), and photos of Mother Teresa and the Qiriazi sisters. He asks Andrra's mother to lend him a book; she says they are for adults and promises them when he is older, adding that one should also read foreign authors to discover other cultures. The text defines culture as a people's language, religion, customs, dress, food, music and arts.

85.title: Cultures Are Diverse (illustration)
85.summary: Full-page illustration for the birthday story: children in party hats cheer around a table with a birthday cake with candles, cupcakes, biscuits, cups and jugs of juice, with a smiling woman (Andrra's mother) standing behind them. The living room is decorated with balloons and bunting and has a sofa, TV and a bookshelf.

86.title: Cultural Institutions
86.summary: A fourth-grade class visits the capital Prishtina with their teacher, and on the bus ride home each child says what impressed them: Rron liked the Puppet Theatre, Albana the Museum of Kosovo where she learned about ancestors and history, and Bora the architecture of the National Library 'Pjetër Bogdani', where she hopes to study as a medical student. They also saw the National Theatre and the Art Gallery. Pictures show these Prishtina buildings.

87.title: Cultural Institutions (continued)
87.summary: Explains that cultural institutions — museums, theatres, cinemas, libraries and galleries — preserve, promote and pass on a community's cultural heritage and knowledge. People visit museums to learn history, theatres to watch actors on stage, cinemas to see films, libraries to read books and galleries to see art exhibitions such as paintings.

88.title: Traditional Clothing
88.summary: Klea and her parents spend a weekend in Boga in the Accursed Mountains (Bjeshkët e Nemuna). On the way home her mother tells her about the traditional costume of the Rugova region, its colours and handwork, and Klea decides to look up traditional costumes online and present them to her class. Pictures illustrate the mountain landscape and regional folk dress.

89.title: Traditional Clothing (continued)
89.summary: Explains that each region has its own traditional costume inherited from the past, such as those of Rugova, Has and Tropoja; women's costumes feature embroidery and bright colours (red dominates in Has), while men wear woollen trousers (tirq), shirt, waistcoat and the white plis cap. Costumes are worn on holidays and celebrations. Two photos show the Rugova costume and the Drenica costume.

90.title: Taking Part in a Celebration
90.summary: Nea invites her classmates Teo and Ami to her sister's wedding held at their home, asking some to carry the bride's dress and others flowers; the family has decorated the living room and prepared sweets and food. While Teo gets ready, his mother reminds him to respect the family's preparations, arrive on time and bring a gift. Pictures illustrate a home wedding celebration with children as guests.

91.title: Taking Part in a Celebration (continued)
91.summary: Discussion questions on decorating for a party, gifts, and how to behave as a guest and as a host. The text explains that a holiday is a special joyful day with special food and clothes, gifts, dancing and singing, and lists types: personal (birthday), state (Kosovo's Independence), national (Albania's Independence celebrated by Albanians everywhere), international (Women's Day) and religious.

92.title: Using Natural Resources
92.summary: Klea asks her friend Rita for help writing an informative article on Kosovo's natural resources. Rita lists above-ground resources (farmland, rivers for drinking water and irrigation, artificial lakes, forests for heating and wood products, many plant species) and underground resources (lignite coal burned in the 'Kosova' power plant, lead from the Trepça mines in Mitrovica, ores). Pictures illustrate the two girls talking and these resources.

93.title: Using Natural Resources (continued)
93.summary: Four captioned photographs show the Mirusha Waterfalls, Badovc Lake, the White Drin river and Batllava Lake. Pupils discuss what Kosovo is rich in and name a river or artificial lake near them. The text defines natural resources and says Kosovo, though small, has farmland for grain, vegetables and fruit, as well as rivers, lakes, forests and underground wealth.

94.title: Using Underground Resources
94.summary: A tour guide welcomes a group of Japanese tourists (who greet him with 'Konnichiwa') and asks why they chose Kosovo; they are researching the underground resources of European countries for a website. The guide explains that Kosovo has large lignite coal reserves used in the 'Kosova A' and 'Kosova B' power plants, and lead, zinc, silver and gold ores, with Trepça in Mitrovica the most active mine. Pictures illustrate the guide with the tourists and mining/power plant scenes.

95.title: Using Underground Resources (continued)
95.summary: Defines underground resources as rocks, minerals, ores and fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) extracted from the earth. Kosovo is rich in coal for electricity and in lead from the Trepça mines, and there is interest in finding natural gas. These resources are non-renewable and must be used sensibly.

96.title: Using Above-Ground Resources
96.summary: Aldi was too tired to follow the lesson, so his classmate Rona explains above-ground resources again: over half of Kosovo is farmland, the rest forested mountains (Accursed Mountains, Sharr, Pashtrik), plus timber that must be cut in a controlled way, and waters — lakes, rivers (the White Drin is the longest), and mineral and thermal healing spas. The text lists lakes (Radoniq, Gazivoda, Batllava, Përlepnica, Badovc), rivers (White Drin, Lepenc, Morava, Ibër) and spas (Peja, Banjska, Kllokot).

97.title: Using Above-Ground Resources (illustration)
97.summary: Full-page illustration for the lesson: a boy in a yellow top and a girl in an orange top (Aldi and Rona) sit chatting on rocks beside a lake, with green hills, pine forest and white red-roofed houses behind them. It shows the above-ground resources discussed: land, forest, mountains and water. Only the key words are printed on the page.

98.title: Sensible Use of Natural Resources
98.summary: After the last school bell, two classmates, Mali and Klea, work on an assignment about protecting natural resources. They discuss renewable and non-renewable sources, propose using more solar panels and wind turbines because coal, oil and gas run out and pollute the air, and suggest planting trees and holding school sessions on saving water and electricity. Pictures illustrate the two children and renewable energy (solar panels, wind turbines).

99.title: Sensible Use of Natural Resources (continued)
99.summary: Summarises that natural resources divide into renewable (sun, air/wind) and non-renewable (coal, oil, natural gas, and water). Uncontrolled use exhausts them and pollutes the environment, so the world is moving towards energy from sunlight and wind.

100.title: Human Resources
100.summary: Rona finds a puzzle in a magazine: sort a set of pictures into two groups, natural resources and human resources. The page shows ten picture tiles: a river, a teacher at a board, a chef, the sun, a doctor, a tree, a red flower, a fir tree, a bricklayer building a wall, and a policewoman.

101.title: Human Resources (continued)
101.summary: Shows Rona's solution in a two-column table: natural resources (sun, waters, forests, plants) versus human resources (doctors, teachers, police officers, bricklayers). Pupils add more examples, look out of the window to list natural resources, and write what human resources their family members represent. The text explains that human resources are a country's workforce and its knowledge and skills, the main driver of economic development.

102.title: We Protect Cultural Heritage
102.summary: The Gashi family spends a weekend in the city of Prizren, where 10-year-old Jonila is fascinated by the old buildings, museums and fortress. Her father, a craftsman from Gjakova, explains that cultural heritage includes parks, galleries, fortresses, stone tower houses (kulla), religious monuments, narrow lanes and fountains, as well as intangible heritage such as language and folk creations; he names the ancient city of Ulpiana, Deçan Monastery and the House of the League of Prizren. Pictures illustrate the father and daughter and these monuments.

103.title: We Protect Cultural Heritage (continued)
103.summary: Describes Kosovo's material heritage: archaeological sites, fortresses, tower houses, churches, mosques, cobbled lanes, fountains and seven active museums (National History Museum, Ethnological Museum 'Emin Gjiku', the Prizren museum in a former Turkish bath), plus the Adem Jashari Memorial Complex, Ulpiana, Deçan Monastery and the League of Prizren house. Intangible heritage covers language and folk creations, and traditional clothing and food also have a special place. These sites are protected by law.

104.title: Health Care
104.summary: A boy named Mali goes to bed after midnight, gets up at 7, rushes to school without breakfast, and after school eats lunch, draws the curtains and naps instead of joining friends who call him to play football outside. When he wakes he eats fast food and drinks fizzy drinks, eats at irregular times and drinks little water, so he looks pale and unhealthy. His worried parents decide to change his habits. Pictures illustrate Mali's unhealthy routine.

105.title: Health Care (continued)
105.summary: Pupils discuss why Mali is pale and unhealthy, talk about their favourite food, explain the saying 'Sport develops body and mind' and write a piece of advice for Mali. The text says staying healthy needs personal hygiene, healthy food, physical activity and sport, walks in fresh air, at least eight hours of sleep, and regular visits to the dentist and family doctor.

106.title: We Help Keep the Environment Clean
106.summary: A teacher asks each pupil how they can help keep the environment clean. Eri suggests walking, cycling or taking the bus because cars pollute the air; Ema talks about recycling waste and using the right bins; Klea about saving water, not littering rivers and not leaving taps running; Mali about planting trees. Pictures illustrate the classroom discussion and these green actions.

107.title: We Help Keep the Environment Clean (continued)
107.summary: Pupils write what should be done to protect the soil, the water and the air in a three-part chart (Land / Water / Air) and compare with a classmate. The text says every citizen is responsible for protecting the environment: save energy, cycle or use public transport, sort waste, save water and plant greenery — and if you cannot protect nature, at least do not destroy it.

108.title: Field Trip: My Country's Natural Riches
108.summary: A planning activity: pupils plan a class excursion around Kosovo, listing with a partner places with natural resources, places of natural beauty (example given: the White Drin river) and places of cultural heritage (example: the League of Prizren). They then write which places they chose to visit and why.

109.title: Field Trip: Planning the Timetable
109.summary: Continuation of the excursion activity: pupils plan the travel schedule for one day of the trip. The page is just an illustration of a blank spiral-bound notepad with lines to write the timetable on.

110.title: People Protect Nature
110.summary: A girl named Era is leafing through an Albanian dictionary and stops at the definition of 'nature' as the environment where people and all living and non-living things exist. She reflects aloud on how wrong it is to litter streets, forests and the sea, harming sea creatures, and asks why people drop rubbish instead of using bins, cut trees instead of planting them, and do not recycle plastic bottles. She decides to give a class presentation on protecting nature.

111.title: People Protect Nature (continued)
111.summary: Pupils say what 'nature' means, which actions Era considers harmful, and sort waste according to the colours of recycling bins (pictures of coloured bins and waste items). The text explains that pollution changes soil, water and air and harms living things, so people must care for nature daily, individually and together.

112.title: Water Pollution
112.summary: Mali spends every spring holiday with his uncles in the village and loves everything there except the village river, into which residents throw rubbish that smells bad. He proposes to his village friends that they clear the litter near the river and ask the adults to help; while collecting rubbish with the villagers, he and his friend Klea recall seeing the sea full of plastic bags and food waste last summer, and their friend Ylli says people must stop. The text explains water pollution, its harm to plants and animals, and sewage as a main pollutant.

113.title: Water Pollution (illustration)
113.summary: Full-page illustration for the river clean-up story: three children on a green riverbank under a bright sun — a boy in red holding a grey rubbish sack, a girl in orange raking up plastic bottles, and a boy in yellow holding a bottle. Behind them are the river with litter floating in it, fields, trees and two red-roofed village houses.

114.title: Soil Pollution
114.summary: A teacher lets pupils choose any project topic; Klea, torn between a favourite animal, a plant and the human body, realises all three live on Earth and decides to research planet Earth. Struck by the fact that Earth is the only one of the eight planets where life is possible, she changes her project to raise classmates' awareness of harmful things children do: dropping litter, wasting water, not recycling. Pictures illustrate Klea researching and planet Earth.

115.title: Soil Pollution (continued)
115.summary: Questions on what makes Earth different from other planets, what we can plant, and what actions pollute the soil; pupils split into groups to plan cleaning the schoolyard. The text says Earth is the only planet in the Solar System with life and people must care for it by planting plants and saplings, recycling and putting rubbish in the right place.

116.title: Let's Protect the Land and Forests
116.summary: While his teacher presents the benefits of trees and photosynthesis, Mali remembers walking in a forest with his family last year and meeting an acquaintance cutting down trees. When Mali told him it was bad for the air, the man replied that this work feeds his family. Mali tells the teacher, who asks what the man could do to make up for the damage — plant a new tree for each one cut. Pictures illustrate the woodcutter in the forest and tree planting.

117.title: Let's Protect the Land and Forests (continued)
117.summary: Pupils discuss the woodcutter's action, Mali's view and the teacher's answer, and think of another solution. The text describes the forest as a perfect 'ecological factory' that cleans the air and shelters wild animals; forests are cut for roads and settlements or burn in summer fires, so we must replant, foresters must look after them, and cutting requires a permit.

118.title: Public and Ecological Transport
118.summary: Klea often talks at home about protecting the environment. Driving with her parents to her grandparents in another town, she notices a long yellow bus with some passengers standing and asks why they travel that way; her father asks whether they are helping or harming the environment, and she realises that if each took a car more fuel would be burned. Her mother explains public transport (timetable, fixed route, standard fare) and Klea suggests the family use it from now on.

119.title: Public and Ecological Transport (continued)
119.summary: Questions on what public transport is, how to behave on it and why ecological transport matters. The text describes urban and intercity public transport run by public and private companies using buses, minibuses and taxis, and ecological transport such as the metro that reduces air pollution; overuse of cars contributes to global warming.

120.title: How Is Waste Recycled?
120.summary: Mali has noticed symbols on the rubbish bin in the schoolyard and heard of the '3R' rule — reuse, recycle, reduce. His teacher explains that waste must be sorted, not thrown in one bin: reuse the same school bag for years by decorating it, give away toys and clothes, and put only plastic bottles, clean paper, glass bottles and drink cans in bins with the recycling sign, at home too. Pictures illustrate recycling bins and sorted waste.

121.title: How Is Waste Recycled? (illustration)
121.summary: Full-page illustration for the recycling lesson: a teacher stands in front of a green chalkboard talking to five pupils seated around a round table in a classroom with bookshelves and a clock. In the foreground are four recycling bins in red, green, blue and yellow, each with the recycling symbol.

122.title: Caring for Hygiene in the Community
122.summary: Mira, who studies piano at the music school, invites her friends to a school concert; the teacher reminds them to arrive on time, sit quietly and listen. While waiting in the corridor, Ylli finishes his snack and drops the wrapper on the floor, and Diellza does the same with her cake wrapper; the teacher and classmates notice, and a boy named Lumi urges everyone to keep public places as clean as they keep themselves. The text says citizens should care for shared spaces as if they were their own.

123.title: Caring for Hygiene in the Community (illustration)
123.summary: Two illustrations for the concert story. Top: a girl (Mira) plays a black grand piano on a stage with red curtains. Bottom: in the concert hall, in front of the stage and red seats, a girl in orange and a boy in yellow each put a crumpled paper wrapper into a small black bin — showing the right behaviour.

124.title: Our Project: A Clean and Green Environment
124.summary: A class project in four working groups to clean up the neighbourhood or shared space, each writing an action plan. Group one plants saplings in the chosen area; group two removes the rubbish from it. Blank spaces are left for the plans.

125.title: Our Project: A Clean and Green Environment (continued)
125.summary: The remaining two project groups write their action plans: group three sorts rubbish into the correct recycling bins, and group four makes lampshades from various recycled materials. Blank spaces are left for the plans.

126.title: Game: Me and You
126.summary: A two-player revision board game: the teacher prepares labels numbered 1–20, each pupil draws one and answers the matching question, scoring two points per correct answer. The questions run along a path across this page and the next; this page has the rules, the 'Me' and 'You' score areas and questions 1 and 16–20 (what is bullying, cultural institutions, Kosovo's underground resources, human resources, what you do for a clean environment, recyclable materials).

127.title: Game: Me and You (question board)
127.summary: Second half of the revision game board with questions 2–15 reviewing the whole book: the smallest social group, volunteering, children's rights and responsibilities, resolving disagreements, cultural diversity, hospitality, solidarity, gender equality, tolerance, Kosovo's regions, the date of independence, the communities represented by the stars on the flag, traditional versus modern family, and Kosovo athletes who won gold medals.

128.title: References
128.summary: A list of web links (Wikipedia, news and travel sites) used as sources for biographies and photographs in the book, such as Mati Logoreci, Sevasti Qiriazi, Majlinda Kelmendi, Ymer Riza, Nexhmije Pagarusha, the National Library and the National Gallery of Kosovo. No lesson content or illustrations.
